objective: Provide an expert-level, implementation-oriented outline of JavaScript covering the ECMAScript language, execution model, types, objects, functions, prototypes, classes, modules, asynchronous programming, promises, iterators, generators, metaprogramming, collections, errors, memory behavior, internationalization, interoperability, runtime environments, tooling, testing, performance, security, and production architecture.
scope: Modern ECMAScript with emphasis on ES2020 through current standardized capabilities, while preserving the historical concepts necessary to understand JavaScript's execution model and compatibility constraints. Distinguish the ECMAScript language specification from host environments such as browsers, Node.js, workers, and embedded runtimes.

sections.name: ECMAScript Foundations
sections.purpose: Establish JavaScript syntax, grammar, scripts, modules, statements, expressions, declarations, strict mode, and the ECMAScript execution model.

subsections.name: Execution Contexts
examples: Function invocation creates an execution context containing the function's bindings and execution state.

sections.name: Types and Values
sections.purpose: Explain JavaScript's dynamic type system, primitive values, objects, coercion, equality, and numeric semantics.

sections.name: Coercion, Equality, and Operators
sections.purpose: Model JavaScript's implicit and explicit conversion rules and operator semantics.

sections.name: Variables, Scope, and Closures
sections.purpose: Explain lexical scoping, declarations, hoisting behavior, temporal dead zones, closures, and binding lifetimes.

sections.name: Objects and the Prototype System
sections.purpose: Explain JavaScript objects, property descriptors, prototype chains, property lookup, mutation, and object identity.

sections.name: Functions and Invocation
sections.purpose: Cover function objects, invocation forms, parameters, return values, this binding, arrow functions, recursion, and higher-order programming.

sections.name: Classes and Object-Oriented JavaScript
sections.purpose: Explain class syntax as a structured layer over JavaScript's prototype-based object model.

sections.name: Arrays, Maps, Sets, and Structured Data
sections.purpose: Cover JavaScript's principal built-in collection and structured-data facilities.

sections.name: Iterators and Generators
sections.purpose: Explain JavaScript's iteration protocol and generator-based lazy computation.

sections.name: Modules and Dependency Architecture
sections.purpose: Explain ECMAScript modules, import/export semantics, module resolution concepts, and dependency boundaries.

subsections.name: Static Modules
examples: export function add(a, b) { return a + b; }

sections.name: Asynchronous JavaScript
sections.purpose: Explain promises, async functions, await, microtasks, task scheduling, cancellation patterns, and asynchronous composition.

subsections.name: Async and Await
examples: async function load() { const result = await fetchData(); return result; }

sections.name: Event Loop and Host Environments
sections.purpose: Separate ECMAScript semantics from host-provided scheduling and APIs.

subsections.name: ECMAScript Jobs
examples: Promise callbacks are scheduled asynchronously rather than executed inline.

subsections.name: Host Integration
examples: setTimeout and DOM events are host facilities rather than ECMAScript language primitives.

sections.name: Errors and Exception Handling
sections.purpose: Cover JavaScript exception semantics, built-in error types, asynchronous error propagation, and robust failure handling.

sections.name: Metaprogramming
sections.purpose: Explain JavaScript facilities for intercepting, reflecting upon, and dynamically constructing language behavior.

subsections.name: Proxy
examples: const proxy = new Proxy(target, { get(obj, key) { return obj[key]; } });

sections.name: Memory Management and Garbage Collection
sections.purpose: Explain JavaScript's managed-memory model, reachability, garbage collection behavior, and memory-retention hazards.

subsections.name: Reachability
examples: An object can remain reachable through a closure even when the original application-level reference is gone.

subsections.name: Weak References
examples: WeakMap can associate metadata with objects without strongly retaining those objects.

sections.name: Typed Arrays, ArrayBuffer, and Binary Data
sections.purpose: Explain JavaScript's binary-memory facilities for high-performance data processing and interoperability.

sections.name: Internationalization
sections.purpose: Cover ECMAScript internationalization facilities for locale-aware formatting, collation, numbers, dates, and pluralization.

sections.name: Browser Platform Integration
sections.purpose: Distinguish JavaScript from browser-provided APIs and explain the principal browser execution environment.

sections.name: Server and Runtime Environments
sections.purpose: Explain JavaScript execution outside browsers, especially Node.js-style server runtimes and runtime APIs.

subsections.name: Runtime APIs
examples: Runtime APIs can expose filesystem and operating-system functionality unavailable to ordinary browser JavaScript.

sections.name: Workers and JavaScript Concurrency
sections.purpose: Explain concurrency through independent execution contexts, message passing, shared memory, and atomics.

sections.name: Tooling, Compilation, and Build Systems
sections.purpose: Cover the modern JavaScript development toolchain from source code through bundling, testing, deployment, and diagnostics.

subsections.name: Bundling and Optimization
examples: Dynamic import can form a code-splitting boundary in compatible build systems.

sections.name: Testing and Verification
sections.purpose: Establish testing strategies for JavaScript applications, libraries, asynchronous code, browser behavior, and runtime services.

sections.name: Performance Engineering
sections.purpose: Explain JavaScript performance through profiling, allocation behavior, event-loop scheduling, data structures, JIT compilation, and rendering considerations.

subsections.name: Runtime Optimization
examples: Stable object shapes can help some JavaScript engines optimize property access.

subsections.name: Memory and Responsiveness
examples: Move CPU-heavy independent work to a worker when blocking the main event loop would harm responsiveness.

sections.name: JavaScript Security
sections.purpose: Cover major application and runtime security risks associated with JavaScript execution and web integration.

subsections.name: Web Application Security
examples: Prefer textContent over assigning untrusted content to innerHTML.

subsections.name: Prototype Pollution
examples: Validate untrusted property names before performing recursive object merges.

subsections.name: Supply-Chain Security
examples: Pin and audit production dependencies according to the project's security requirements.

sections.name: Application Architecture and Design Patterns
sections.purpose: Apply JavaScript language and runtime facilities to scalable applications and libraries.

subsections.name: Event-Driven Design
examples: Use explicit event contracts when multiple components communicate asynchronously.

sections.name: Serialization and Interoperability
sections.purpose: Explain data exchange between JavaScript systems, external services, processes, and other programming languages.

subsections.name: WebAssembly Interoperability
examples: JavaScript can load and interact with WebAssembly modules through host APIs.

relationships.relationship: Closures retain access to lexical environments after the surrounding execution context has returned.
Objects participate in prototype-based property lookup.
Class syntax establishes prototype-based relationships rather than replacing the underlying object model.
Functions can capture bindings from their lexical environments.
Promise reactions are scheduled through ECMAScript job mechanisms integrated with host scheduling.
Async functions and await operate through promise-based asynchronous completion.
Static module imports define explicit dependency relationships and module boundaries.
Dynamic module loading can establish lazy-loading boundaries in host build systems.
Weak collections permit associations that do not strongly retain their keys.
Typed arrays provide structured views over binary buffers.
Independent execution contexts communicate through messaging and transferable data.
Atomics provides synchronization operations for shared memory.
Browser APIs extend the ECMAScript language with host capabilities such as DOM, networking, and timers.
Node.js provides a server/runtime host environment around a JavaScript engine.
Prototype mutation and unsafe object merging can create security vulnerabilities such as prototype pollution.
Allocation patterns and object retention can influence garbage-collection workload and application latency.

dependencies.name: ECMAScript specification
dependencies.purpose: Defines JavaScript language semantics, built-in objects, execution behavior, and standard language facilities.

dependencies.name: JavaScript engine
dependencies.purpose: Parses, interprets, compiles, optimizes, and executes JavaScript.

dependencies.name: Host environment
dependencies.purpose: Provides APIs and scheduling mechanisms surrounding the ECMAScript engine.

dependencies.name: Build system
dependencies.purpose: Bundles, transforms, optimizes, tests, and packages application code.

dependencies.name: Debugger and profiler
dependencies.purpose: Provides runtime inspection and performance analysis.

edge_cases.handling: NaN is not equal to itself under ordinary equality; use Number.isNaN or appropriate semantic checks.
Account for the distinction between -0 and +0 where numeric identity matters; Object.is can expose the distinction.
Do not assume decimal arithmetic is exact; use appropriate integer, decimal, tolerance, or domain-specific strategies.
Determine invocation form before reasoning about this; arrow functions capture lexical this.
Treat untrusted property names and object-merging operations defensively.
Avoid unintentionally retaining large object graphs through long-lived callbacks or closures.
Ensure asynchronous failures are explicitly observed or propagated.
Avoid long synchronous CPU operations on responsiveness-sensitive event loops.
Prevent unbounded chains of microtasks from starving host task processing.
JSON.stringify cannot directly serialize arbitrary cyclic object graphs.
Do not implicitly mix BigInt and Number in arithmetic; convert intentionally.
Distinguish missing array elements from explicit undefined values when iteration or serialization semantics matter.
Never rely on finalization for deterministic resource cleanup.
Understand live bindings and module evaluation order when circular dependencies exist.
Treat module loading as an asynchronous operation that can reject.
Do not assume constructors or instanceof checks behave identically across execution realms.
Account for transferred ArrayBuffers becoming detached in the sending context where applicable.

constraints: ECMAScript language semantics must be distinguished from host-specific APIs.
Browser APIs, Node.js APIs, and other runtime APIs are not interchangeable language primitives.
JavaScript uses dynamic typing; static guarantees require additional tooling or language layers.
Object identity and prototype relationships can affect equality, lookup, and security.
Garbage collection does not provide deterministic resource cleanup.
Asynchronous operations must account for promise rejection and scheduling behavior.
CPU-heavy synchronous work can block an event loop in single-threaded host execution contexts.
Shared memory requires careful synchronization and atomic operations.
Security-sensitive code must treat external input as untrusted.
Dependency trees introduce supply-chain risk and require lifecycle management.
Performance behavior is engine- and workload-dependent and should be measured rather than assumed.
Transpilation and bundling can alter deployment artifacts while preserving intended source-level semantics.
Module resolution behavior depends on the host environment and tooling.
Serialization formats define explicit limits on supported JavaScript values and object graphs.

validation.check: Source parses successfully under the intended ECMAScript grammar and runtime.
Primitive conversion, equality, numeric behavior, and object identity match the intended semantics.
Bindings, closures, initialization order, and temporal-dead-zone behavior are correct.
Prototype relationships, property descriptors, getters, setters, and object mutation behave as intended.
Promises, async functions, rejection propagation, and scheduling behavior are explicitly tested.
Long-lived references, caches, closures, event handlers, and worker resources do not create unintended retention.
Worker communication and shared-memory operations use appropriate synchronization and ownership semantics.
External input is validated or safely encoded and known JavaScript/web attack surfaces are addressed.
Module boundaries, exports, imports, cycles, resolution, and deployment behavior are validated.
Required ECMAScript features are supported by the target engines or appropriately transformed.
Critical paths are profiled under representative workloads and event-loop latency is measured where relevant.
Unit, integration, end-to-end, asynchronous, regression, and security tests cover critical behavior.
Production bundles, source maps, environment configuration, dependency locks, and runtime versions are reproducible.

open_questions: Should the next iteration focus exclusively on modern ECMAScript features, or include the historical evolution from ES5 through current ECMAScript?
Should the ECMAScript execution model be expanded into a formal treatment of realms, agents, execution contexts, environment records, references, and abstract operations?
Should the event loop be separated into ECMAScript job semantics and detailed browser versus Node.js scheduling models?
Should JavaScript security be expanded into a dedicated web-security taxonomy covering XSS, CSRF, CSP, Trusted Types, prototype pollution, supply-chain attacks, and sandbox boundaries?
Should the browser platform be expanded into DOM, Web APIs, rendering, storage, networking, workers, service workers, and WebAssembly?
Should Node.js be expanded into filesystem, streams, networking, child processes, worker threads, module resolution, and server architecture?
Should JavaScript performance be expanded into JIT internals, hidden classes, inline caches, garbage collectors, profiling methodology, and benchmark design?
Should TypeScript be treated as a separate language/toolchain layer rather than part of JavaScript itself?
Should frontend architecture be expanded into component systems, state management, routing, hydration, server-side rendering, and client-side rendering?
Should backend architecture be expanded into HTTP services, queues, databases, caching, observability, authentication, authorization, and distributed systems?
